claim: The genomes of 75 isolates of T.b. gambiense Group 1 were sequenced, including multiple samples from geographically separated disease foci within Guinea (n=37), Côte d'Ivoire (n=36) and Cameroon (n=2) collected over fifty years (1952–2004).
source: The genomes of 75 isolates of T.b. gambiense Group 1 (Supplementary file 1) were sequenced, including multiple samples from geographically separated disease foci within Guinea (n=37), Côte d'Ivoire (n=36) and Cameroon (n=2) collected over fifty years (1952–2004).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of isolates sequenced and their geographical and temporal distribution, representing primary data collection.

claim: A total of 230,891 single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) were identified compared to the haploid consensus assembly of the T.b. brucei reference genome.
source: A total of 230,891 single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) were identified compared to the haploid consensus assembly of the T.b. brucei reference genome (Berriman et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the number of SNPs identified through genomic analysis, supported by the reference to the genome used for comparison.

claim: T.b. gambiense Group 1 showed a 5–10 fold lower number of SNPs and SNP density compared to the other groups.
source: T.b. gambiense Group 1 showed a 5–10 fold lower number of SNPs (11,398) and SNP density compared to the other groups (Figure 1—source data 1), despite an over-representation in terms of the number of samples.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data comparing SNP numbers across groups, with reference to source data.

claim: T.b. gambiense Group 1 genotypes showed an extremely low level of intra-group diversity, with the two most distantly related isolates differing only at 435 SNP loci.
source: Phylogenetic network analysis revealed that T.b. gambiense Group 1 genotypes showed an extremely low level of intra-group diversity (e.g. the two most distantly related isolates differed only at 435 SNP loci) and formed a monophyletic group (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from phylogenetic analysis with specific quantitative data on SNP differences.

claim: T.b. gambiense Group 1 forms a monophyletic group.
source: Phylogenetic network analysis revealed that T.b. gambiense Group 1 genotypes showed an extremely low level of intra-group diversity (e.g. the two most distantly related isolates differed only at 435 SNP loci) and formed a monophyletic group (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a direct statement based on phylogenetic network analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The network features reticulation among non-Group 1 parasites indicating the presence of recombinant genotypes.
source: The network features reticulation among non-Group 1 parasites indicating the presence of recombinant genotypes; this stands in contrast to Group 1 parasites and is consistent with an absence, or rarity, of recombination in this group.
evidence: This is an interpretation of phylogenetic network patterns, inferring recombination from reticulation patterns.

claim: The T.b. gambiense Group 1 population is geographically sub-structured.
source: Network analysis of T.b. gambiense Group 1 revealed the population is geographically sub-structured (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from network analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A significant deviation from Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium (HWE) was observed at 97.4% of SNP loci (P<10-17 at each locus).
source: A significant deviation from Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium (HWE) was observed at 97.4% of SNP loci (P<10-17 at each locus) and this was found to be associated with every sampled genotype being heterozygous at these loci (Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This is a statistical result from population genetic analysis with specific P-values and percentages.

claim: Every sampled genotype was heterozygous at loci showing deviation from Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium.
source: A significant deviation from Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium (HWE) was observed at 97.4% of SNP loci (P<10-17 at each locus) and this was found to be associated with every sampled genotype being heterozygous at these loci (Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This is a direct observation from genotype data analysis.

claim: FIS was calculated for each SNP locus, giving a uni-modal distribution with a median of -1.
source: FIS was calculated for each SNP locus, giving a uni-modal distribution with a median of -1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Figure 1—source data 3), as would be predicted for a strictly asexual population.
evidence: This is a statistical result from population genetic analysis with reference to figures showing the distribution.

claim: A median FIS of -1 is predicted for a strictly asexual population.
source: FIS was calculated for each SNP locus, giving a uni-modal distribution with a median of -1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Figure 1—source data 3), as would be predicted for a strictly asexual population.
evidence: This is a statement based on established population genetics theory.

claim: Strong evidence of linkage disequilibrium (LD) was obtained for each chromosome using a genome-wide panel of SNP loci.
source: Using a genome-wide panel of SNP loci, strong evidence of linkage disequilibrium (LD) was obtained for each chromosome and the whole genome formed a single genetic linkage group (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a direct result from linkage disequilibrium analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The whole genome of T.b. gambiense Group 1 formed a single genetic linkage group.
source: Using a genome-wide panel of SNP loci, strong evidence of linkage disequilibrium (LD) was obtained for each chromosome and the whole genome formed a single genetic linkage group (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a direct result from linkage disequilibrium analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Multiple long tracts of homozygosity, termed Loss of Heterozygosity (LOH), were identified across the genome of Group 1 isolates.
source: Inspection of the SNP distribution across the genome of Group 1 isolates identified multiple long tracts of homozygosity, termed Loss of Heterozygosity (LOH) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from genomic analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: LOH is not due to the loss of part of a homologue and is consistent with mitotic gene conversion.
source: Examination of read depth variation confirmed that this is not due to the loss of part of a homologue and is consistent with mitotic gene conversion; similarly there is no evidence of aneuploidy.
evidence: This is an inference based on read depth analysis, ruling out alternative explanations.

claim: There is no evidence of aneuploidy in T.b. gambiense Group 1.
source: Examination of read depth variation confirmed that this is not due to the loss of part of a homologue and is consistent with mitotic gene conversion; similarly there is no evidence of aneuploidy.
evidence: This is a direct statement based on read depth analysis.

claim: LOH has occurred on every chromosome in T.b. gambiense Group 1.
source: In T.b. gambiense Group 1, LOH has occurred on every chromosome, with many isolates showing the same LOH patterns (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), strongly suggesting that many of these regions arose early in Group 1 evolution.
evidence: This is a direct observation from genomic analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Many isolates show the same LOH patterns, strongly suggesting that many of these regions arose early in Group 1 evolution.
source: In T.b. gambiense Group 1, LOH has occurred on every chromosome, with many isolates showing the same LOH patterns (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), strongly suggesting that many of these regions arose early in Group 1 evolution.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of shared LOH patterns across isolates.

claim: Chromosome 10 displayed the greatest variation in LOH sites, with a total of eighteen different patterns of variation among Group 1 genomes.
source: Chromosome 10 displayed the greatest variation in LOH sites, with a total of eighteen different patterns of variation among Group 1 genomes (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a direct observation from LOH analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: LOH on Chromosome 10 varied from 2% to 82% of the chromosome length.
source: This varied from 2% to 82% of the chromosome length, with LOH occurring predominantly towards one telomere.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from LOH analysis of Chromosome 10.

claim: LOH on Chromosome 10 occurred predominantly towards one telomere.
source: This varied from 2% to 82% of the chromosome length, with LOH occurring predominantly towards one telomere.
evidence: This is a direct observation of the spatial distribution of LOH on Chromosome 10.

claim: Distinct LOH patterns were associated with particular phylogenetic lineages, indicating LOH has occurred at various points in Group 1 evolution.
source: Distinct LOH patterns were associated with particular phylogenetic lineages, indicating LOH has occurred at various points in Group 1 evolution (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between LOH patterns and phylogenetic relationships shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: T.b. gambiense Group 1 parasites are evolving asexually.
source: Taken together, these analyses clearly demonstrate that Group 1 parasites are evolving asexually.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence including linkage disequilibrium, HWE deviation, and FIS values.

claim: A key predicted feature of asexual diploid species is the independent evolution and divergence of alleles on chromosome homologues.
source: A key predicted feature of asexual diploid species is the independent evolution and divergence of alleles on chromosome homologues (Birky, 1996), often referred to as the 'Meselson effect' (Birky, 1996; Butlin, 2002; Mark Welch and Meselson, 2000).
evidence: This is a statement of established evolutionary theory supported by multiple citations.

claim: For all three manually phased regions, a clear sequence of accumulating mutations could be inferred, with each haplotype evolving independently, thus illustrating the Meselson effect.
source: For all three regions, a clear sequence of the accumulating mutations could be inferred (Figure 3), with each haplotype evolving independently, thus illustrating the Meselson effect (Judson and Normark, 1996).
evidence: This is a direct observation from manual phasing analysis shown in Figure 3, with citation to the Meselson effect concept.

claim: Phylogenetic trees for each chromosome revealed that A and B haplotypes separate into distinctive clusters.
source: Excluding LOH regions, phylogenetic trees for each chromosome were generated, revealing that A and B haplotypes separate into distinctive clusters (example in Figure 4A) and for every chromosome this pattern was maintained (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from phylogenetic analysis shown in Figures 4A and 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: For every chromosome, the pattern of A and B haplotypes separating into distinctive clusters was maintained.
source: Excluding LOH regions, phylogenetic trees for each chromosome were generated, revealing that A and B haplotypes separate into distinctive clusters (example in Figure 4A) and for every chromosome this pattern was maintained (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from phylogenetic analysis across all chromosomes shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Co-phylogenetic analysis revealed congruence between the A and B haplotype trees across different chromosomes.
source: Co-phylogenetic analysis revealed congruence between the A and B haplotype trees across different chromosomes (Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplements 2 and 3) illustrating that these haplotypes are evolving in parallel.
evidence: This is a direct result from co-phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4B and supplementary figures.

claim: A and B haplotypes are evolving in parallel.
source: Co-phylogenetic analysis revealed congruence between the A and B haplotype trees across different chromosomes (Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplements 2 and 3) illustrating that these haplotypes are evolving in parallel.
evidence: This is an inference based on the congruence observed in co-phylogenetic analysis.

claim: A genome-wide mutation rate of 1.82 x 10–8 substitutions per site per year was estimated.
source: A rate of 1.82 x 10–8 substitutions per site per year was estimated, similar to that of the COII-NDI 'clock' locus in T. cruzi (Lewis et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a calculated value based on accumulated mutations and isolation dates, with comparison to a published rate in T. cruzi.

claim: The estimated mutation rate is similar to that of the COII-NDI 'clock' locus in T. cruzi.
source: A rate of 1.82 x 10–8 substitutions per site per year was estimated, similar to that of the COII-NDI 'clock' locus in T. cruzi (Lewis et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a comparison to a published mutation rate in T. cruzi.

claim: The time since the existence of the most recent common ancestor (MRCA) of the Group 1 isolates analysed in the study is estimated to be in excess of one thousand years before present.
source: Given the observed number of accumulated mutations per isolate, the genome size, and our calculated mutation rate, the time since the existence of the most recent common ancestor (MRCA) of the Group 1 isolates analysed in the study is estimated to be in excess of one thousand years before present (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is a calculated estimate based on mutation rate and accumulated mutations.

claim: Using the mutation rates for two different T. cruzi clock genes (COII-NDI and GPI), the date of emergence was estimated to be between 750 and 9,500 years before present.
source: Similarly, using the mutation rates for two different T. cruzi clock genes (COII-NDI and GPI) (Lewis et al., 2011), the date of emergence was estimated to be between 750 and 9,500 years before present (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is a calculated estimate using published mutation rates from T. cruzi.

claim: T.b. gambiense Group 1 reproduces exclusively asexually.
source: We provide robust evidence that this important human parasite reproduces exclusively asexually, demonstrating complete genetic linkage across the genome and the absence of allelic segregation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple lines of genetic evidence including linkage and lack of segregation.

claim: T.b. gambiense Group 1 demonstrates complete genetic linkage across the genome.
source: We provide robust evidence that this important human parasite reproduces exclusively asexually, demonstrating complete genetic linkage across the genome and the absence of allelic segregation.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a genetic observation supporting asexuality.

claim: T.b. gambiense Group 1 shows an absence of allelic segregation.
source: We provide robust evidence that this important human parasite reproduces exclusively asexually, demonstrating complete genetic linkage across the genome and the absence of allelic segregation.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a genetic observation supporting asexuality.

claim: Meiosis-specific genes are intact and expressed in T.b. gambiense Group 1.
source: Despite meiosis-specific genes being intact and expressed (Peacock et al., 2014), the population genetic data is incompatible with sexual reproduction, self-fertilisation, aneuploidy (Schurko et al., 2009), a parasexual cycle (Ramírez and Llewellyn, 2014; Forche et al., 2008) or the atypical meiosis observed in Rotifers (Signorovitch et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement based on a cited study showing gene expression.

claim: The population genetic data is incompatible with sexual reproduction, self-fertilisation, aneuploidy, a parasexual cycle or the atypical meiosis observed in Rotifers.
source: Despite meiosis-specific genes being intact and expressed (Peacock et al., 2014), the population genetic data is incompatible with sexual reproduction, self-fertilisation, aneuploidy (Schurko et al., 2009), a parasexual cycle (Ramírez and Llewellyn, 2014; Forche et al., 2008) or the atypical meiosis observed in Rotifers (Signorovitch et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on population genetic data, ruling out alternative reproductive mechanisms with citations.

claim: The barrier to sexual reproduction in T.b. gambiense Group 1 remains unclear.
source: The barrier to sexual reproduction in T.b. gambiense Group 1 remains unclear.
evidence: This is an explicit statement acknowledging a gap in understanding.

claim: The lack of decay of 'meiosis-associated' genes may be explained by the relatively recent emergence of this asexual lineage, such that insufficient time has elapsed to allow decay.
source: The lack of decay of 'meiosis-associated' genes may be explained by a number of non-mutually exclusive hypotheses including the relatively recent emergence of this asexual lineage, such that insufficient time has elapsed to allow decay.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis to explain an observation.

claim: Meiosis-associated genes may perform additional roles in processes such as DNA repair or VSG-related recombination.
source: Alternatively, these genes may perform additional roles in processes such as DNA repair or VSG-related recombination.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis to explain the maintenance of meiosis genes.

claim: The parasite population comprises just two independently evolving haplotypes.
source: Our data indicates the parasite population comprises just two independently evolving haplotypes; this remarkable observation confirms the Meselson effect at a whole-genome level for the first time.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on haplotype analysis and phylogenetic data.

claim: This study confirms the Meselson effect at a whole-genome level for the first time.
source: Our data indicates the parasite population comprises just two independently evolving haplotypes; this remarkable observation confirms the Meselson effect at a whole-genome level for the first time.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty and significance of the findings.

claim: The original report of the Meselson effect focused on Bdelliod rotifers but was later shown to be due to cryptic tetraploidy.
source: The original report of the Meselson effect focused on Bdelliod rotifers (Welch, 2000), however this was later shown to instead be due to the entirely different phenomenon of cryptic tetraploidy (Mark Welch et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a statement about previous research findings with citations.

claim: In Daphnia, the relatively high rate of mitotic recombination in comparison to the mutation rate results in novel heterozygous sites being eliminated by gene conversion (LOH) events much faster than they are generated and consequently allelic divergence is not observed.
source: The relatively high rate of mitotic recombination in comparison to the mutation rate results in novel heterozygous sites being eliminated by gene conversion (LOH) events much faster than they are generated and consequently allelic divergence is not observed (Omilian et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a statement about findings in another organism with citation.

claim: In Timema stick insects, nuclear alleles display a higher level of divergence in asexual rather than sexual species.
source: More recently, in the genome of Timema stick insects, nuclear alleles have been shown to display a higher level of divergence in asexual rather than sexual species (Schwander et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a statement about findings in another organism with citation.

claim: In T.b. gambiense Group 1, the mitotic recombination rate is sufficiently low so as not to obscure the pattern of accumulating mutations.
source: In that system, as in T.b. gambiense Group 1, the mitotic recombination rate is sufficiently low so as not to obscure the pattern of accumulating mutations, and this has underpinned our ability to detect and confirm the Meselson effect.
evidence: This is an inference about the mitotic recombination rate based on the ability to detect the Meselson effect.

claim: T.b. gambiense Group 1 emerged from a single progenitor.
source: The similarity of the genomes studied from different geographical locations, together with a lack of recombination in the evolution of T.b. gambiense Group 1, suggests this sub-species emerged from a single progenitor.
evidence: This is an inference based on genome similarity and lack of recombination.

claim: Each clade represents a separate country and these are partitioned by the earliest branches of the phylogenetic tree, implying early radiation and colonisation.
source: Each clade represents a separate country and these are partitioned by the earliest branches of the phylogenetic tree, implying early radiation and colonisation.
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic tree structure and geographical distribution.

claim: The emergence of T.b. gambiense Group 1 within the last 10,000 years coincided with an important period in human history when civilisation and livestock farming were developing in West Africa.
source: The emergence of T.b. gambiense Group 1 within the last 10,000 years coincided with an important period in human history when civilisation and livestock farming were developing in West Africa (Oliver, 1966), but whether asexual reproduction was a prerequisite for human infection or occurred subsequently is uncertain.
evidence: This is a temporal correlation with historical context, with citation and acknowledgment of uncertainty about causation.

claim: Whether asexual reproduction was a prerequisite for human infection or occurred subsequently is uncertain.
source: The emergence of T.b. gambiense Group 1 within the last 10,000 years coincided with an important period in human history when civilisation and livestock farming were developing in West Africa (Oliver, 1966), but whether asexual reproduction was a prerequisite for human infection or occurred subsequently is uncertain.
evidence: This is an explicit statement of uncertainty about the temporal relationship between asexuality and human infectivity.

claim: The successful asexual human pathogen T.b. gambiense Group 1 contrasts markedly with the virtually extinct sexual T.b. gambiense Group 2 parasite that occupied similar biological and geographical niches.
source: This successful asexual human pathogen contrasts markedly with the virtually extinct sexual T.b. gambiense Group 2 parasite that occupied similar biological and geographical niches and this may be an example of the dominance of an asexual lineage over its sexual counterpart (Charlesworth, 1980).
evidence: This is a comparative observation with speculation about evolutionary dynamics, supported by citation.

claim: The extensive loss of heterozygosity across large regions of each chromosome likely arose from gene conversion/mitotic recombination.
source: Another remarkable feature of the T.b. gambiense Group 1 genome is the extensive loss of heterozygosity across large regions of each chromosome, which likely arose from gene conversion/mitotic recombination.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism underlying LOH based on genomic patterns.

claim: Gene conversion provides a mechanism for removing a proportion of deleterious mutations in asexual eukaryotes.
source: Gene conversion provides a mechanism for removing a proportion of deleterious mutations in asexual eukaryotes, as hypothesised in other systems (Tucker et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement of a hypothesis with citation to work in other systems.

claim: A fitter allele on one haplotype would be positively selected, resulting in long-range tracts of LOH that encompass the loci under selection together with extensive flanking regions.
source: A fitter allele on one haplotype would be positively selected, resulting in long-range tracts of LOH that encompass the loci under selection together with extensive flanking regions.
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis to explain the observed LOH patterns.

claim: Following an LOH event, individuals will experience a slight decline in long-term fitness due to newfound homozygosity featuring pre-existing sub-optimal alleles, leaving a signature equivalent to inbreeding.
source: However, it has been predicted that following an LOH event, individuals will experience a slight decline in long-term fitness due to newfound homozygosity featuring pre-existing sub-optimal alleles, leaving a signature equivalent to inbreeding (Tucker et al., 2013) in the progeny.
evidence: This is a statement of a prediction from cited work.

claim: LOH may be a more powerful evolutionary force than the accumulation of point mutations and thus may drive Muller's Ratchet more quickly than de novo mutations.
source: This process has been described as a more powerful evolutionary force than the accumulation of point mutations (Omilian et al., 2006) and thus may drive Muller's Ratchet more quickly than de novo mutations.
evidence: This is a statement combining cited work with speculation about evolutionary dynamics.

claim: Although LOH may effectively counteract the accumulating mutational load in the short-term, it is unclear whether it can prevent this uniquely well-adapted pathogen from ultimately entering an extinction vortex.
source: This suggests that although LOH may effectively counteract the accumulating mutational load in the short-term, it is unclear whether it can prevent this uniquely well-adapted pathogen from ultimately entering an extinction vortex.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about long-term evolutionary consequences.

claim: T.b. gambiense Group 1 is the main causative agent of human African trypanosomiasis.
source: Here we investigate the reproductive strategy of a putatively asexual yet successful human pathogen, Trypanosoma brucei gambiense Group 1, the main causative agent of human African trypanosomiasis, which contrasts with closely-related, sexually reproducing sub-species.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about the disease.

claim: T.b. gambiense Group 1, found in West and Central Africa, causes >97% of all human cases of trypanosomiasis.
source: T.b. gambiense Group 1, found in West and Central Africa, is the main human-infective sub-species, causing >97% of all human cases of trypanosomiasis (Simarro et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a statement of epidemiological data with citation.

claim: T.b. gambiense Group 2 was detected in the 1980/90s in Côte d'Ivoire and Burkina Faso but may now be extinct.
source: T.b. gambiense Group 2 was detected in the 1980/90s in Côte d'Ivoire and Burkina Faso but may now be extinct (Capewell et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about the status of Group 2 with citation.

claim: T.b. rhodesiense is found in East Africa and causes <3% of human cases.
source: A third human infective sub-species, T.b. rhodesiense, is found in East Africa and causes <3% of human cases (Simarro et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a statement of epidemiological data with citation.

claim: Each of the human infective sub-species appears to have arisen independently from the non-human infective T. brucei.
source: Each of these human infective sub-species appears to have arisen independently from the non-human infective T. brucei and possesses a different mechanism of human infectivity (Capewell et al., 2013; Capewell et al., 2011; Uzureau et al., 2013; Van Xong et al., 1998).
evidence: This is a statement about evolutionary origins with multiple citations.

claim: Each human infective sub-species possesses a different mechanism of human infectivity.
source: Each of these human infective sub-species appears to have arisen independently from the non-human infective T. brucei and possesses a different mechanism of human infectivity (Capewell et al., 2013; Capewell et al., 2011; Uzureau et al., 2013; Van Xong et al., 1998).
evidence: This is a statement about mechanisms of infectivity with multiple citations.

claim: All sub-species of T. brucei, with the important exception of T.b. gambiense Group 1, show evidence for mating in natural populations.
source: All sub-species of T. brucei, with the important exception of T.b. gambiense Group 1, show evidence for mating in natural populations (Capewell et al., 2013; Duffy et al., 2013; Gibson and Stevens, 1999) and have the ability to undergo sexual reproduction with Mendelian allelic segregation and independent assortment of unlinked markers (Cooper et al., 2008; MacLeod et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a statement about reproductive biology with multiple citations.

claim: All sub-species of T. brucei except T.b. gambiense Group 1 have the ability to undergo sexual reproduction with Mendelian allelic segregation and independent assortment of unlinked markers.
source: All sub-species of T. brucei, with the important exception of T.b. gambiense Group 1, show evidence for mating in natural populations (Capewell et al., 2013; Duffy et al., 2013; Gibson and Stevens, 1999) and have the ability to undergo sexual reproduction with Mendelian allelic segregation and independent assortment of unlinked markers (Cooper et al., 2008; MacLeod et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a statement about reproductive biology with citations.

claim: Haploid gametes have been observed in T.b. brucei.
source: In addition, haploid gametes have been observed in T.b. brucei (Peacock et al., 2014) and although meiosis genes appear to be expressed in T.b. gambiense Group 1 (Peacock et al., 2014), no haploid gametes have ever been observed in these parasites (Peacock et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement of an observation with citation.

claim: No haploid gametes have ever been observed in T.b. gambiense Group 1 parasites.
source: In addition, haploid gametes have been observed in T.b. brucei (Peacock et al., 2014) and although meiosis genes appear to be expressed in T.b. gambiense Group 1 (Peacock et al., 2014), no haploid gametes have ever been observed in these parasites (Peacock et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement of an observation with citation.

claim: The absence of haploid gametes in T.b. gambiense Group 1 is consistent with clonality in all Group 1 populations analysed.
source: This is consistent with clonality in all Group 1 populations analysed (Koffi et al., 2009; Morrison et al., 2008; Tibayrenc and Ayala, 2012), however, these studies were based on limited sets of genetic markers, which lack the necessary discriminatory power to distinguish between predominantly clonal evolution, with occasional bouts of genetic exchange, and strictly asexual propagation.
evidence: This is a statement connecting observations to previous findings with citations, while noting limitations.

claim: Previous studies of T.b. gambiense Group 1 clonality were based on limited sets of genetic markers, which lack the necessary discriminatory power to distinguish between predominantly clonal evolution, with occasional bouts of genetic exchange, and strictly asexual propagation.
source: This is consistent with clonality in all Group 1 populations analysed (Koffi et al., 2009; Morrison et al., 2008; Tibayrenc and Ayala, 2012), however, these studies were based on limited sets of genetic markers, which lack the necessary discriminatory power to distinguish between predominantly clonal evolution, with occasional bouts of genetic exchange, and strictly asexual propagation.
evidence: This is a critique of previous studies with citations.

claim: Genomic-level analyses of T. brucei diversity to date have concentrated on T.b. brucei and T.b. rhodesiense.
source: Genomic-level analyses of T. brucei diversity to date have concentrated on T.b. brucei and T.b. rhodesiense and for T.b. gambiense Group 1, include only the genome reference strain (DAL972) (Goodhead et al., 2013) or two (Sistrom et al., 2014) field isolates.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field with citations.

claim: For T.b. gambiense Group 1, previous genomic analyses included only the genome reference strain (DAL972) or two field isolates.
source: Genomic-level analyses of T. brucei diversity to date have concentrated on T.b. brucei and T.b. rhodesiense and for T.b. gambiense Group 1, include only the genome reference strain (DAL972) (Goodhead et al., 2013) or two (Sistrom et al., 2014) field isolates.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field with citations.

claim: The T. brucei genome is approximately 26 Mb in size and comprises eleven major chromosomes between one and six megabases together with an array of intermediate and mini-chromosomes.
source: The T. brucei genome is approximately 26 Mb in size and comprises eleven major chromosomes between one and six megabases together with an array of intermediate and mini-chromosomes (Ogbadoyi et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a statement of established genomic knowledge with citation.

claim: SNPs were evenly distributed over the eleven major chromosomes, covering 85% of the genome.
source: These were evenly distributed over the eleven major chromosomes, covering 85% of the genome (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from SNP distribution analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Obligate asexual reproduction has been argued to carry considerable negative evolutionary consequences.
source: Obligate asexual reproduction has been argued to carry considerable negative evolutionary consequences (Maynard Smith, 1986) hence most clonal species undergo some degree of recombination, albeit infrequent, which generates novel genotypes (Heitman, 2006).
evidence: This is a statement of evolutionary theory with citations.

claim: Most clonal species undergo some degree of recombination, albeit infrequent, which generates novel genotypes.
source: Obligate asexual reproduction has been argued to carry considerable negative evolutionary consequences (Maynard Smith, 1986) hence most clonal species undergo some degree of recombination, albeit infrequent, which generates novel genotypes (Heitman, 2006).
evidence: This is a statement of evolutionary theory with citation.

claim: The study demonstrates the Meselson effect for the first time at the genome-wide level in any organism.
source: We demonstrate the Meselson effect for the first time at the genome-wide level in any organism and show large regions of loss of heterozygosity, which we hypothesise to be a short-term compensatory mechanism for counteracting deleterious mutations.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty and significance of the findings from the abstract.

claim: Large regions of loss of heterozygosity are hypothesised to be a short-term compensatory mechanism for counteracting deleterious mutations.
source: We demonstrate the Meselson effect for the first time at the genome-wide level in any organism and show large regions of loss of heterozygosity, which we hypothesise to be a short-term compensatory mechanism for counteracting deleterious mutations.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their observations.

claim: T.b. gambiense is derived from a single progenitor, which emerged within the last 10,000 years.
source: We determine that T.b. gambiense is evolving strictly asexually and is derived from a single progenitor, which emerged within the last 10,000 years.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the abstract based on genomic and dating analyses.

claim: T.b. gambiense is evolving strictly asexually.
source: We determine that T.b. gambiense is evolving strictly asexually and is derived from a single progenitor, which emerged within the last 10,000 years.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the abstract based on population genetic analyses.
